strengths: FoNE offers a simple, compact numerical representation and a parallel digit decoder. Encoding an entire number as one token addresses a meaningful efficiency limitation of conventional numerical tokenization.

The reported arithmetic improvements are substantial: perfect accuracy on large held-out sets for several tasks, strong data and parameter efficiency, and measured training and inference speedups. Comparisons include digit-wise tokenization, subword tokenization, xVal, fine-tuned Llama, and NTL.

The evaluation extends beyond short arithmetic through 60-digit addition, experiments with a second transformer architecture, and three-seed evidence that Fourier digit embeddings improve Abacus length generalization.
The FineWeb pretraining and continual-pretraining experiments provide useful initial evidence that numerical embeddings can coexist with language modeling.
weaknesses: The experiments do not adequately isolate the central Fourier contribution. FoNE changes input encoding, sequence length, output factorization, and supervision simultaneously. Crucially, the direct-digit ablation uses RMSE rather than FoNE's classification objective (Appendix H.1). A concatenated one-hot or learned digit representation with the same single-token interface and parallel classification head is needed to establish whether Fourier features drive the gains.

The normalization justification is substantially overstated. Lemma D.2 assumes zero-mean inputs, orthogonal positional embeddings, and unit-norm FoNE vectors, although Definition 3.2 gives norm sqrt(m+n). These assumptions are not established for the actual input containing learned [NUM] embeddings or a learned projection. Orthogonality alone also does not make coordinate-pair ratios of the sum equal those of FoNE. The proof therefore does not justify the general claim that the representation is unaffected by LayerNorm.

Claims of representing all numbers without range limitations exceed the method's scope. With fixed m and n, the encoding is periodic with period 10^m, and the decoder produces only a fixed number of nonnegative decimal digits. Signed outputs, overflow, and precision outside the configured range are not specified. Chunking addresses long-input numerical precision but does not remove fixed representational capacity.

The language-model evidence requires more careful controls. Overall token perplexities across different tokenizations and numerical prediction objectives are not directly comparable. The text-only evaluation is more informative, but equal budgets of 10B tokens need not expose models to equal amounts of raw text. The continual-pretraining experiment retains BPE and uses a simplified embedding adaptation, so its MMLU result does not validate the full single-token encoder and decoder.

Generalization evidence for the full method remains limited. The 97.42% long-addition result averages across operand lengths seen within a training range extending to 60 digits; it is not evidence of extrapolation beyond that range. The Abacus extrapolation experiment uses digit-wise tokens instead of full-number tokens. No downstream numerical reasoning benchmark establishes the broader practical benefits claimed.

Reproducibility and reliability remain incomplete: the main scaling experiments lack seed variability, and the language-model experiments omit important parser, precision, loss-weighting, and training details. Several explanations also conflict with the evidence—for example, Appendix B describes base-5 inputs with period 8 as performing poorly, while Table 7 reports 99.97%. Together with the missing controlled baselines, these issues prevent the otherwise promising results from meeting the acceptance threshold.

strengths: FoNE is a simple, computationally attractive representation: multiscale sinusoidal features encode a bounded-precision number in one token, and a parallel digit-classification head avoids autoregressive digit generation.

The reported arithmetic gains are substantial. These include 99% decimal-addition accuracy with 6,400 examples, perfect accuracy on several large held-out sets, and lower training and inference times than digit-wise and subword baselines.

The evaluation extends beyond basic arithmetic through classification, modular addition, 60-digit addition, Abacus integration across three seeds, and language-model pretraining. Comparisons with xVal and Number Token Loss provide useful additional context.
weaknesses: The experiments do not adequately isolate the contribution of Fourier input features from single-token compression and parallel digit classification. Crucially, the direct-digit ablation uses RMSE loss and regression decoding (Appendix H.1), whereas FoNE uses digit-wise cross-entropy. Its weaker performance therefore does not establish the necessity of sinusoidal encoding. A packed learned or one-hot digit representation with the same classification head, loss, and training budget is an essential missing control.

The language-modeling evidence does not establish the claimed improvement in semantic abilities. Figure 5 compares perplexity across different tokenizations and output objectives, which are not directly comparable. Table 5's text-only evaluation helps, but does not clearly establish identical evaluated text positions, comparable raw-data exposure, or matched compute. MMLU evaluates only the simplified BPE-preserving adaptation, rather than the complete single-token method.

The normalization argument is substantially narrower than the claims made from it. Lemma D.2 assumes zero mean and orthogonal positional encodings, and its proof additionally assumes unit-norm FoNE vectors, although the defined representation has norm sqrt(m+n). These conditions are not established for the actual embeddings, which include learned token embeddings and potentially a learned projection. The proof therefore does not justify general invariance to LayerNorm or RMSNorm in the implemented architecture.

Claims of representing all numbers and eliminating range limitations are overstated. With fixed m and n, the embedding repeats with period 10^m, and the decoder outputs a fixed number of nonnegative decimal digits. Signed outputs, overflow, and values beyond the selected precision are not adequately specified. Chunking addresses floating-point precision for long inputs, but still requires an explicitly bounded representation.

The strongest scalability and generalization claims exceed the evidence. The 60-digit experiment trains on operand lengths up to 60 digits and reports an average across length pairs, rather than demonstrating extrapolation by the complete single-token method. The Abacus extrapolation experiment is encouraging, but uses digit-wise tokens. Neither establishes unrestricted length generalization for the proposed primary architecture.

Experimental reporting leaves consequential uncertainties. Most central arithmetic comparisons lack seed variation or uncertainty estimates, and the newer pretraining experiments omit sufficient optimization and numeric-loss details for reproduction. There are also explicit inconsistencies: Appendix B describes period-8 performance on base-5 inputs as poor, while Table 7 reports 99.97%. These issues, together with the missing controlled ablations, make the evidence insufficient for acceptance despite the promising results.

strengths: FoNE offers a simple, useful design combining multiscale Fourier number embeddings with parallel digit classification, representing and generating a bounded-precision number in one token.

The reported arithmetic gains are substantial: 99% accuracy on six-digit decimal addition with 6,400 examples, perfect accuracy on large held-out sets for several tasks, and meaningful training and inference speedups.
Evaluation includes multiple operations, model and dataset sizes, a second architecture, NTL comparisons, and three-seed experiments showing improved length generalization when combined with Abacus.
The 10B-token pretraining experiments and continual-pretraining arithmetic improvements provide encouraging evidence beyond isolated synthetic arithmetic.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate Fourier encoding from single-token compression and parallel digit supervision. A matched single-token baseline using concatenated learned or one-hot digit embeddings with the same classification decoder is missing. The direct-digit ablation instead uses RMSE (Appendix H.1), confounding the representation and loss.

Language-model evidence needs stronger controls. Perplexities across different tokenizations are not directly comparable, and equal token budgets can expose models to different amounts of raw text. Table 5's text-only evaluation helps, but identical evaluation targets and matched training text are not established. The continual-pretraining experiment retains BPE and therefore does not validate the complete single-token method.

The normalization argument overreaches. Lemma D.2 assumes zero-mean inputs and orthogonal positional encodings, then introduces unit-norm assumptions that do not match the defined multiscale embedding. These conditions are not established for the implemented embeddings, including the added learned [NUM] vector; the lemma therefore does not justify the general normalization-robustness claim.

Claims of eliminating range limitations require qualification. Fixed m and n impose range and precision limits, the embedding repeats modulo 10^m, and the decoder does not specify signed outputs. The 60-digit experiment trains on lengths up to 60 and reports an average across length pairs; it does not demonstrate unseen-length generalization of the full single-token method.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting remain incomplete: most central curves lack multiple-seed statistics, and the large pretraining experiments omit important implementation and optimization details. These gaps, together with the missing matched baseline, leave the promising contribution slightly below the acceptance threshold.
